facts.claim: At a Jewish wedding the badeken (bedeken, veiling) follows the pre-chupah receptions: a procession led by the groom goes to the bride's reception room, where the groom covers the bride's face with a veil.
facts.quote: After the short pre-chupah receptions hosted by the bride and groom, the badeken ceremony commences. A procession headed by the groom goes to the bridal reception room, where the groom covers the bride's face with a veil.

facts.claim: After the groom veils the bride, the fathers and grandfathers of the bride and groom bless her; her face stays veiled for the whole chupah ceremony, giving her privacy at this holy time.
facts.quote: After the groom veils the bride, the fathers and grandfathers of the bride and groom approach the bride and bless her. ... The bride's face remains veiled for the duration of the chupah ceremony, affording her a bit of privacy at this holy time.

facts.claim: Chabad.org traces the custom of veiling the bride's face to the Matriarch Rebecca, who covered her face when meeting her groom, Isaac.
facts.quote: The custom of covering the bride's face with a veil originated with our Matriarch Rebecca, who covered her face with a handkerchief when meeting her groom, Isaac.

facts.claim: Chabad.org gives the veil's meaning as the groom valuing the bride's inner beauty, which never fades, rather than only her external beauty.
facts.quote: The veil emphasizes that the groom is not solely interested in the bride's external beauty, which fades with time; but rather in her inner beauty which she will never lose.

facts.claim: In Chassidic custom the badeken veil is dense enough to fully hide the bride's face and has no silver or gold threads, as bride and groom wear no jewellery to the chupah.
facts.quote: Chassidic custom is for the veil to be dense enough to completely obscure the bride's face. It also should not contain any silver or gold threads, as the bride and groom do not wear any jewelry to the chupah

facts.claim: A Honiton lace veil worn in London in February 1865 was designed so its pattern shows on the outside when the veil is folded over.
facts.quote: The bride's veil has been skilfully designed so that the pattern is on the outside when the veil is folded over.

facts.claim: The V&A's label for a Devon Honiton lace veil of about 1850 says the bride would have worn it attached to the back of her head, not over her face, a fashion which came later; its pea-pod pattern is a symbol of fruitfulness and happiness.
facts.quote: The pattern of this Honiton lace veil includes pea-pods, which are symbols of fruitfulness and happiness. The bride would have worn the veil attached to the back of her head, not over her face, a fashion which came later.
facts.conflicts: Read via api.vam.ac.uk/v2/museumobject/O171447. Overlaps batch A (Victorian section); batch A owns Queen Victoria facts.

facts.claim: The 1865 veil, dress and boots were kept in the bride's family: the V&A records them as worn by the donor's mother and bequeathed by her daughter in 1947.
facts.quote: This dress, veil and a pair of boots ... were worn by Eliza Penelope Bright, nee Clay (the mother of the donor) for her marriage to Joseph Bright ... Bequeathed by Miss H. G. Bright
facts.conflicts: The record shows the veil kept by the next generation, not re-worn by a later bride; do not claim reuse.

facts.claim: A 1902 veil in the V&A was worn with a wax orange blossom hair ornament and hair piece arranged on the head together with the veil.
facts.quote: the museum also holds the wax orange blossom hair ornament and hair piece worn by the bride ... which would have been arranged on the head in conjunction with the veil.

insider_details.detail: If a Jewish ceremony is planned, build the badeken into the run sheet as its own moment before the chupah: the groom veils the bride in her reception room with family present, so allow a separate space and time near the ceremony site, and agree with the officiant how dense the veil should be.
A veil that will be folded forward as a blusher should be checked for which side the pattern sits on when folded; period lace veils were designed for exactly this.

An heirloom veil is often a family keepsake rather than something worn by every generation; ask early whether a family veil is wearable or only to be carried or displayed, so there is time to plan a headpiece around it.
Carry an heirloom veil in hand luggage rather than checked bags, and check how your travel policy treats items in checked baggage and unattended items.

On a clifftop or beach, plan to wear the veil for the ceremony and photographs and take it off for the reception; secure it to the hair or headpiece, and have someone ready to lift and settle it in the wind. (Practical advice, not a sourced fact.)
